To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a three-dose MTaT approach reduced asymptomatic Plasmodium infection prevalence, but did not reduce malaria transmission.
(1) community-based MTaT reduces malaria transmission in a high-transmission setting, and (2) MTaT is cost-effective.

(1) a community-based approach to mass testing and treatment of malaria in western Kenya reduced malaria transmission as measured by entomological and serological indices and reduced clinical malaria incidence; (2) this approach was feasible and acceptable to the communities in which it was implemented; and (3) the cost of this approach was approximately US $1.00 per person tested and treated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of community-based approaches for malaria transmission reduction.
the evaluation of a community-based approach to malaria control that has potential to reduce malaria transmission in an area of very high transmission intensity.
the impact of a community-based MTaT intervention on the incidence of malaria in the population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study design and methods described in this manuscript are adequate to evaluate the effect of a MTaT strategy on the incidence of symptomatic and asymptomatic malaria, and on malaria transmission, in a setting of high transmission intensity.
the study is a cluster-randomized trial of community-based MTaT for malaria in an endemic setting.

this trial is designed to evaluate the effect of community-based intermittent mass testing for malaria on the prevalence and incidence of Plasmodium falciparum infections, malaria morbidity and entomological parameters in an area of intense transmission.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
community-based mass testing and treatment of malaria is an effective and feasible strategy for reducing malaria transmission.
the MTaT approach reduced the incidence of clinical malaria and asymptomatic malaria infections, and that the effect of MTaT on transmission was sustained for at least 6 months.
the MTaT approach is a promising approach for malaria elimination, and the study design described here is an effective approach for measuring the effects of such interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cluster randomization is an effective method to reduce confounding in studies evaluating malaria transmission.

cluster randomized trials can be conducted in malaria endemic areas, even in the absence of a functioning national health information system, if careful attention is paid to the design and implementation of the trial.

the design and implementation of community-based trials for malaria transmission reduction require careful attention to the study design, including the selection and size of clusters, the timing and frequency of intervention, the use of multiple study endpoints, and the need to account for the effects of other malaria interventions that may be implemented during the study period.
